title: 136 Million Barrels of Oil Got Through the 'Closed' Strait of Hormuz. The Market Is Just Finding Out.
excerpt: Dark tankers, switched-off transponders and 'goat paths' along the Omani coastline kept crude flowing while the world watched the blockade. Oil has crashed to a two-month low.
body:
When Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz "closed" in late February, the world braced for the worst energy crisis in a generation. Brent crude spiked to nearly $120 a barrel. Analysts warned it was just the beginning. Forecasts of $200 oil made headlines.

Three and a half months later, Brent has crashed below $86 — its lowest in nearly two months — and the mystery of why oil never went where everyone said it would is being answered by data that tells a story of quiet defiance, switched-off transponders and maritime ingenuity.

## The numbers behind the curtain

Shipping data firm Kpler estimates that roughly 136 million barrels of non-Iranian crude moved through the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman export channels between the start of April and June 10 — about 1.9 million barrels a day.

"After an initial disruption at the onset of the conflict, flows strengthened as alternative logistics scaled up," Kpler said.

Those "alternative logistics" were not subtle. Iraq, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates exported large quantities of crude in tankers running with their automatic identification systems switched off — sometimes in arrangements with Iran, sometimes without, according to trading sources who spoke to Reuters.

The result: millions of barrels moving through waters that were nominally closed to all traffic, invisible to conventional vessel-tracking platforms but visible in the physical oil market, where supply never dropped as far as the headlines implied.

## Trump's 'secret mission' claim

U.S. President Donald Trump added his own twist on Wednesday, saying for the first time that a secret American mission had escorted "more than 100 million barrels of oil" through the strait. "That's why it's at $85, $90 a barrel, instead of $250," he told reporters.

The 100-million-barrel figure is broadly consistent with the Kpler data, though analysts note the picture is more complex than either side presents. Dark tanker movements, shuttle transfers between vessels and transhipments off the Omani coast — what traders have taken to calling "goat paths" — have all played a role in keeping crude flowing.

Matt Smith, Kpler's U.S. lead analyst, told MarketWatch that combining Persian Gulf transits via Hormuz and Gulf of Oman crude exports of unknown origin captures "both direct Hormuz movements and Gulf of Oman-linked flows that may involve dark transits, shuttle tanker movements or offshore transfers."

## Why oil is crashing now

The immediate catalyst for Friday's plunge is the prospect of a formal U.S.-Iran deal. A senior administration official put the odds of signing a memorandum of understanding in the coming days at 80 to 85 per cent. The deal would formally reopen the strait, lift the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports and begin releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets.

But the Kpler data suggests the market's risk premium was already built on shaky ground. If 1.9 million barrels a day were already getting through, the actual supply shortfall was far smaller than feared — and the price was already carrying a premium for a disruption that never fully materialised.

Brent crude fell more than 3 per cent on Friday, dipping below $86. WTI traded near $84. Both benchmarks are well below the $90-to-$107 band that prevailed during the height of the conflict and are approaching levels that fundamentals alone would justify.

## What it means for India

For India, the world's third-largest oil importer, the slide from $120 to below $86 is not an abstraction. Every dollar off the price of a barrel saves the country roughly $2.1 billion a year on its import bill.

At $120, HSBC had projected India's balance of payments deficit would balloon to $65 billion in the current fiscal year. At current levels, the deficit looks far more manageable. The rupee has already recovered from its May low near 97 to the 94.50-to-96.00 range. Inflation, which hit a new-series high of 3.93 per cent in May, faces less upward pressure from fuel prices if crude stays in the mid-80s.

The RBI has built its entire recent policy package — subsidised dollar deposits, cheap hedging for overseas borrowings, tax cuts for foreign bond investors — on the assumption that oil would remain expensive. If prices continue to fall, some of those emergency measures may prove to have been insurance that was not needed, but insurance that still reshaped India's capital markets for the better.

For NRIs who have watched their remittance value shrink as the rupee weakened, cheaper oil is the single biggest variable that could reverse the trend. A sustained drop below $85 would do more for the rupee than any central bank intervention.
